system:
You are the Arabic language reviewer, standing in for an Arabic reviewer at the issuing authority. You compare the Arabic text with the English text and report any difference in meaning: numbers, times, places, the hazard, and above all the protective action. You cannot approve the Arabic; a named person who reads Arabic still must.
You see only the English and Arabic headline, description and instruction, and how the Arabic was produced. You cannot approve or send the alert; people decide.

Review the alert within your mandate only. Decide:
- "agree": nothing within your mandate is wrong;
- "object": something is wrong and the drafter can fix it (say how in `fix`);
- "escalate": something is wrong that needs a decision by a person or a higher authority.

Every objection needs evidence. Each evidence item is a word-for-word quote (at least 5 words for a
clause, at least 3 for the alert or inputs) from either a knowledge base clause shown to you (kind
"clause", ref = its id) or the material you were shown (kind "view", ref = the field name). Quotes are
checked by code; an objection with no quote that matches is thrown away. Do not object to things
outside your mandate. Do not repeat the same issue twice. Issues listed under `recorded_gaps` are already
reported to the approvers on every alert; do not object to them again.
If you have a concern but none of the clauses shown supports it, put it in `no_basis` instead.

For every objection also fill `uae_basis`: if one of the UAE clauses shown (ids starting with ITU-UAE:, TDRA-,
UAE-, DXB-) speaks to this issue, set status "cites_uae" with its id and a word-for-word quote; otherwise set
status "none_applies" with empty ref and quote. Say "none_applies" honestly: it tells the regulator where UAE
texts are silent.

5 EU-Alert capabilities 5.1 Language The need to support Public Warning Messages in various languages is necessary for the European Public Warning System because there are many European countries that share borders where there is a frequent and significant movement of mobile subscribers across those borders, i.e. a high instance of international roaming. Emergency messages should be sent out to users in their own language but when not practicable, then in the language of the message originator. It is impractical to determine the language of the user and so messages shall be sent out in the native language of the country originating the message and subject to national requirements, in any other language or languages that the originator chooses. A CBS structure is required to accommodate the requirement to broadcast messages in multiple languages virtually simultaneously in order not to disadvantage any recipient of a message in a particular language. ETSI TS 123 041 [1] contains an assignment of Message Identifiers for EU-Alert messages in the local language, which is the same range as for CMAS messages in English. data.summary: The Arabic matches the English in meaning. Headline: heavy rain at times, Saturday 13:30 to 21:00. Description: convective clouds, light to moderate rain that may become heavy at times, eastern, southern and western areas and parts of the interior, Saturday 22 August, 13:30 to 21:00. Instruction: take care outdoors or driving while it rains, follow official updates at the same URL. Numbers, times, places and the protective action are the same. The Arabic was machine translated, so a named Arabic reader must still approve it before sending. I cannot approve it.

no_basis.concern: The Arabic was machine translated. Two minor points for the human Arabic approver: 'NCM' is left in Latin script in the Arabic text, and the weekday is given in the Arabic without the English 'Saturday' appearing twice. Neither changes the meaning.
no_basis.searched_for: UAE requirement on Arabic naming of the issuing authority or on machine-translated alert text
